extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, marketers, and communications writers creating press release headlines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing effective press release headlines that drive engagement and SEO by using clear messaging, strong action verbs, specific details, and appropriate length/keyword placement. Includes recommended headline approaches and explicit avoidances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and main point
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear and state the main point directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the core news or claim up front so readers immediately understand the announcement. Avoid ambiguity or burying the main point behind extraneous words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong active verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active verbs like 'launches' or 'reveals' to add energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer high-impact verbs (revolutionize, accelerate, empower, transform, simplify, enhance) and data-driven recommendations such as 'Allow,' 'Reveal,' and 'Show' which are more attractive. 'Unveil' and 'reveal' get more engagement than 'launch.' Replace weak verbs (announced, launched) with stronger alternatives (unveils, reveals, debuts). Headlines with strong active verbs drive 25% more clicks than passive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include numbers and specifics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete specifics such as large numbers, dates, dollar amounts to signal significance (e.g., milestones, user counts, funding amounts). Milestone headlines should include large specific numbers + active verbs like 'Surpasses' to signal momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer 'why it matters' (benefit-led focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer 'why it matters' by focusing on benefits or outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the benefit or outcome for the audience rather than product features. Use a benefit-led approach to make the headline relevant and compelling (e.g., show how the announcement solves a real problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with company name or primary subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with company name or primary subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the organization or key subject at the beginning when appropriate to establish context and authority—especially for announcement-style headlines (company name + action + specific noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include keywords for SEO and place them early
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the most important keywords within the first 55–70 characters to improve search relevance. Ensure headline wording aligns with likely search queries while remaining clear and natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and character performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines between 51–75 characters perform best for engagement; generally keep headlines under 100 characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the 51–75 character sweet spot for clicks and readability. Stay under 100 characters as a hard limit and prioritize placing key words early (first 55–70 characters) for SEO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Present tense is standard ('launches,' 'announces'); avoid past tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present-tense verbs to make the news feel current and active. Avoid past-tense constructions that can make announcements seem stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended structures: Problem/solution; Milestone; Announcement; Benefit-led.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Problem/solution: identify a widespread problem and present the solution (e.g., 'Remote Team Communication Challenges — New App Solves...'). 2) Milestone: highlight a specific number or achievement with an active verb (e.g., 'Surpasses'). 3) Announcement: company name + strong action verb + specific noun. 4) Benefit-led: focus on audience outcome. Choose the approach that best fits the news and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don'ts / avoidances
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include hyperlinks in headlines (hurts SEO). Don't use clickbait, jargon, unnecessary adjectives, or exceed 100 characters. Keep language simple, truthful, and focused on the core message.
